assertion_results.text: The plan uses Rust's idiomatic null guard patterns for each field — unwrap_or_default(), as_ref(), map(), or if-let/match — rather than calling .unwrap() directly
assertion_results.evidence: plan.md lines 125-138 show: cves uses 'as_ref().map(|v| v.clone()).unwrap_or_default()', affected_packages uses 'as_ref().map(|pkgs| pkgs.len() as u32).unwrap_or(0)', severity_counts uses 'as_ref().cloned().unwrap_or_default()'. Line 154 states 'No direct .unwrap() calls — all paths handle None gracefully'. null-guards.md line 90 confirms 'No .unwrap() or .expect() calls are used anywhere in the implementation.'

assertion_results.text: The plan does NOT access any of the three Option fields without a guard — no direct .len(), .join(), or iteration on Option<T> without unwrapping safely
assertion_results.evidence: In plan.md lines 125-138, all three Option fields are accessed through guard chains: cves via as_ref().map().unwrap_or_default(), affected_packages via as_ref().map().unwrap_or(0), severity_counts via as_ref().cloned().unwrap_or_default(). The .len() call on affected_packages (line 131) is inside a map() closure operating on the unwrapped inner Vec, not on the Option itself. null-guards.md lines 55-56 explicitly notes: 'Direct .len() on the Option — Option<Vec<T>> does not have a .len() method' as a pattern NOT used.

assertion_results.text: The null guards analysis explains why defensive access is needed: the data crosses a module boundary from the ingestor module, and the producer's schema allows None values
